other_uses: The most drought- and heat-tolerant cultivated bean in the world, grown by the Tohono O'odham, Akimel O'odham and Hopi on summer flood-water fields for at least a thousand years. It sets a crop on rainfall that would kill a common bean, and it is native to the southwestern United States. A nitrogen-fixing legume: it partners with rhizobia to pull nitrogen out of the air, which is why beans were planted with corn and squash rather than beside them. Native range: Arizona, New Mexico and Texas south into Sonora, Chihuahua and Jalisco.
prep: Soak and boil like any dry bean; teparies are small, dense and take longer than common beans. The flavour is sweeter and nuttier.
harvest: Dry pods 60–90 days from sowing; harvest before they shatter.
soil: Well-drained, moderately fertile soil; beans resent heavy nitrogen feeding.
risks: Never eat Phaseolus seeds raw or undercooked. They contain phytohaemagglutinin, a lectin that causes violent vomiting and diarrhoea — a few raw beans is enough. Soak, discard the water, and boil hard for at least ten minutes; a slow cooker alone does not reach a safe temperature.
